content_voiceover: Now the animation advances to show the rest of the pathway fully lit up. Fibrin monomers have self assembled, overlapping in that half staggered D to E to D pattern, into the fibrin polymer you see in the middle of the slide, this is a soft clot at this stage, held together only by noncovalent D E interactions, and it's mechanically weak. To stabilize it, thrombin also activates factor thirteen into factor thirteen a, shown here converting on the left side of the slide. Factor thirteen a is a transglutaminase, and it catalyzes covalent cross-links between the gamma chains, and to a lesser extent the alpha chains, of adjacent D domains on neighboring fibrin monomers. Those covalent bonds are what convert the soft, noncovalently associated polymer into the cross-linked fibrin polymer shown at the bottom, which is mechanically much stronger and resistant to fibrinolysis. This is a classic board topic, remember that factor thirteen deficiency causes a clinically distinct bleeding pattern, delayed bleeding with poor wound healing, because the initial soft clot forms normally but it's unstable and falls apart.
keypoints: Fibrin monomers self-assemble into a soft, noncovalent fibrin polymer
Thrombin also activates factor XIII into factor XIIIa, a transglutaminase
FXIIIa cross-links gamma chains (and some alpha chains) between D domains
Cross-linking converts soft polymer into stable, mechanically strong clot
Factor XIII deficiency causes delayed bleeding with poor wound healing
keypoint_voiceover: Fibrin monomers self assemble into a soft polymer first, then thrombin-activated factor thirteen a cross-links the gamma chains between D domains, converting it into a strong, stable clot. Remember factor thirteen deficiency for boards, it presents with delayed bleeding and poor wound healing because the initial clot is unstable.
